units.title: Tasting and Seasoning
units.blurb: The basic tastes, salt, acid, fat and heat, herbs and spices, and how to taste and adjust.

units.title: Seasons and Menus
units.blurb: Cooking with the seasons and writing a menu.

topics.title: The Basic Tastes and Aroma
topics.short: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami are tasted on the tongue; most of what we call flavor is aroma, smelled from the back of the mouth.
topics.trouble: People think the tongue has a map with one taste per zone; each taste can be sensed all over the tongue.

topics.title: Seasoning: Salt, Acid, Fat and Heat
topics.short: Salt makes food taste more like itself, acid brightens, fat carries flavor, and heat (both chile and cooking) adds depth. Season in layers.
topics.trouble: Cooks add all the salt at the end, when it sits on the surface instead of seasoning through.

topics.title: Tasting and Adjusting
topics.short: Taste with a clean spoon every time, often; fix flat with salt or acid, too salty with more unsalted base, too sour with sweetness or fat.
topics.trouble: Cooks double-dip a tasting spoon, or try to fix too much salt by adding sugar.

topics.title: Herbs, Spices and Aromatics
topics.short: Hardy herbs go in early and tender herbs at the end; toast whole spices to wake them; about 1 part dried herb replaces 3 parts fresh.
topics.trouble: Cooks add tender basil at the start of a long simmer, so its flavor is gone by serving time.

topics.title: Seasonality and Sourcing
topics.short: Food tastes best and costs least at the height of its season; menus change with what farms and markets have.
topics.trouble: People write a menu that needs ripe tomatoes in winter.

topics.title: Writing a Menu
topics.short: Balance the menu in methods, colors, richness and station load; describe dishes honestly; price from food cost; and look at what sells.
topics.trouble: New chefs put five fried dishes on one menu, all from one overloaded station.
